checks.name: a1-scope-boundary-declared-before-any-code
checks.summary: SCOPE BOUNDARY, written before any code was edited. ROW 1 -- what this task makes true: the working directory an Invocation declares actually becomes the child process's working directory, so a Provider whose command line carries no path (claude) runs in the Increment's workspace instead of wherever the Runner was started. ROW 2 -- what it deliberately does not do: it adds, removes and reorders no mount (the confinement's two mount pairs are byte-identical before and after, asserted); it widens nothing the child may reach (a directory outside the confined workspace is refused, never accommodated); it removes no directory flag any CLI's own help declares (codex keeps -C, opencode keeps --dir); and it changes nothing about what environment a child receives. ROW 3 -- what it records but does not fix: provider.Invocation's second unconsumed field, Environment (dp-v2-077 d8). Grant.Apply writes it, only FakeInvocationRunner observes it, and SupervisedInvocationRunner.Run builds the child environment itself from the approved record's base names. Recorded, escalated, not changed. ROW 4 -- what only V2-028 can establish: that codex and opencode accept a directory flag alongside an inherited working directory, or refuse when both are supplied. Neither CLI has an authenticated session on this machine and measuring it needs a run subcommand, which this task's rules forbid. ROW 5 -- this task passes no release gate and satisfies no M6 completion condition.

checks.name: a6-rejected-ordering-measured-with-a-positive-control
checks.summary: MEASUREMENT with two admissible outcomes, taken on kernel 6.18.33.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2 (linux/amd64). The rejected ordering was expressed exactly as os/exec expresses it: wrap with no in-namespace cd, and the cwd supplied through the Cmd's own Dir, which chdirs in the forked child before unshare execs and therefore before either mount pair exists. MEASURED RESULT: the rejected ordering ACTUALLY PERMITS the write the seal was meant to stop -- the relative upward write exited 0 with empty stderr and the file REACHED THE HOST FILESYSTEM outside the workspace. So the rejected ordering is not merely unprovable; on this kernel it is demonstrably exploitable. POSITIVE CONTROL on an identical workspace: the chosen ordering (in-namespace cd after both mount pairs) put the child in the workspace and refused the identical upward relative write, leaving nothing behind, which is what makes the comparison informative. The design was NOT changed on the basis of this result -- it was already settled by dp-v2-077 d4's structural argument -- and the test was not adjusted to agree with the packet.
